title: Art Forms in Nature, Plate 49: Actiniae

image.credit: collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: Many sea anemones are arranged together on one page, each with a soft body and rings of tentacles that spread outward like flower petals. The shapes repeat in different sizes and poses, forming a patterned, almost decorative design.

source.museum: collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, public-domain statement)

context: A lithography print made by Ernst Haeckel in 1904 as one plate in his Art Forms in Nature series. Actiniae is the Latin group name for sea anemones, sea animals whose tentacles spread around a central mouth.

descriptions.k: These are sea animals called sea anemones. Their arms spread out like flower petals. Look at all the little arms. Which sea anemone is your favorite? Why do you like it?
descriptions.g12: Ernst Haeckel made this print of sea animals called sea anemones. Their soft arms spread out in circles, a bit like flowers. He put many of them on one page. Look for shapes that repeat. Which ones look alike, and which look different?
descriptions.g35: This print by Ernst Haeckel shows sea anemones, which scientists call Actiniae. It is Plate 49 from his Art Forms in Nature series and was made in 1904 using lithography. Haeckel studied living things closely, yet he also arranged them like a pattern. Choose one anemone and describe its shape. How do the tentacles repeat?
descriptions.g68: Haeckel's Plate 49 (1904) is a scientific illustration that also works as a design. Sea anemones, grouped under the name Actiniae, are shown with radiating tentacles and curving bodies, and the page arranges many forms into one balanced composition. Lithography allowed fine detail and many printed tones. Is this picture mainly for science, for beauty, or both? Use what you see to decide.
descriptions.g910: Plate 49 from Haeckel's Art Forms in Nature (1904) presents Actiniae as repeating, radiating forms. The page balances accurate observation with deliberate arrangement, so scientific study and visual pattern overlap. Lithography supports the fine gradations that make the soft bodies convincing. How does the layout guide your eyes, and where does the plate seem to prioritize design over documentation? Consider what repetition and variation add to your answer.
descriptions.g1112: Haeckel's Plate 49 (1904) sits at the meeting point of natural history and design. The Actiniae are shown with strong radial symmetry, and the plate arranges them as an ornamental whole. Art historians often link the series with the visual culture of its day, and its claims about nature have also been debated. How does the presentation shape what we accept as objective, and what might a purely documentary image look like?

k.daily: Find the anemone with the most arms. How many parts do you think it has?
k.emotion: How do these sea animals make you feel? Do they seem calm or busy?
k.observation: Point to one anemone. What parts can you name on it?
k.analysis: Which anemones are big and which are small on this page?
k.line: Trace one tentacle with your finger. Does it curl, bend or go straight?
k.shape: Look for circle shapes. Where do the arms make a ring?
k.color: Which colors do you see most on the page? Where do they appear?
k.texture: Imagine touching a sea anemone. Would it feel soft or hard? Why do you think so?
k.space: Which anemone seems closest to you, and which one seems farther back?
k.light: Where do you see light spots and dark spots on the soft bodies?
k.meaning: Why do you think someone drew sea animals so carefully?
k.culture: These animals live in the sea. What would you tell a friend who has never seen one?

k.critical: If you could add one more animal to this page, what would it be and where would it go?

g12.daily: How can you tell these animals have no bones or hard shells just by looking?

g12.shape: Where do you see round shapes, and where do you see long skinny shapes?
g12.color: How do the colors help you tell one part of an anemone from another?
g12.texture: How did the artist show that the bodies look wet and smooth?
g12.space: How do the overlapping shapes make some anemones look in front of others?
g12.light: Where does the page look brightest, and how does that help you see the shapes?
g12.meaning: What might Haeckel want people to feel about small sea animals when they look at this print?
g12.culture: How could a picture like this help people who live far from the sea learn about it?
g12.technique: Haeckel printed this from a stone using lithography. What clues show you this is a print and not a photograph?
g12.personal: If you could look at a real anemone in water, what would you want to watch for?
g12.critical: Why might this page belong in a science book and also on an art poster? Tell what you see.

g35.daily: Which details show that Haeckel looked closely at these sea animals? Point to two.

g35.line: How do the curving lines of the tentacles move your eyes around the plate?
g35.shape: Which shapes repeat across the page, and how does repeating them create a pattern?
g35.color: How do the different tones and colors separate the tentacles from the bodies?
g35.texture: What marks does the lithograph use to suggest the squishy, wet texture of the animals?
g35.space: How does the artist overlap and size the anemones to make the page feel deep?
g35.light: How do lighter and darker areas make the tentacles look rounded rather than flat?
g35.meaning: Why might a scientist choose to show many types of one animal on the same page?

g68.daily: Which choices in this plate suggest it was designed to be looked at, and not only studied?
g68.emotion: How does the radial arrangement of tentacles create a feeling of calm or of motion for you?

g68.color: How do the color relationships help clarify the parts of each animal and unify the page?

g68.space: How do overlaps and different scales build a sense of space on a flat sheet?
g68.light: How does tonal modeling give the soft forms volume and make them seem alive?
g68.meaning: What might the artist want us to understand about the beauty of ordinary sea creatures?
g68.culture: How might scientific illustration in 1904 differ from the way we show animals with cameras today?
g68.technique: What advantages did lithography offer for reproducing detailed natural forms in many copies?
g68.personal: Which design decisions would you borrow if you made your own plate about an animal you know?
g68.critical: How can one image be both accurate and artistic? Make your case with specific parts of this plate.

g910.daily: Which specific features show scientific study, and which show decorative arrangement, in the Actiniae?
g910.emotion: How does the symmetry and repetition shape the emotional tone, which can feel serene or slightly eerie?
g910.observation: Examine how the tentacles attach to the body. What does this detail tell you about the artist's observation?

g910.line: How do the rhythm of curved lines and the density of tentacle marks create energy across the sheet?
g910.shape: How does repeated radiating geometry turn living animals into ornament?
g910.color: How does the palette separate individual forms while holding the entire plate together?
g910.texture: How does the lithographic process produce tonal softness that suggests flesh rather than hard shell?
g910.space: How do overlap, scale shift and spacing between forms create layered depth on the page?
g910.light: How does the handling of light on tentacles and bodies suggest translucency?
g910.meaning: How does the plate frame nature as something ordered and beautiful, and what does that framing leave out?
g910.culture: How does a 1904 scientific print show the connection between art, science and publishing at that time?
g910.technique: What does a lithographic stone allow that a woodcut would not, based on the fineness of line here?
g910.personal: What does this plate make you reconsider about the line between scientific and artistic images?
g910.critical: How might the beauty of this plate influence how persuasive its scientific claims feel, and is that influence fair?

g1112.daily: How does Plate 49 hold scientific description and aesthetic arrangement in tension, and which one leads?
g1112.emotion: In what ways does the plate's symmetry invite awe, and might it also impose order that nature lacks?
g1112.observation: Scan the junctions where tentacles meet bodies. What do they reveal about observation versus idealization?
g1112.analysis: How does the compositional hierarchy of the plate reflect an assumption about how knowledge should be organized?
g1112.line: How do the line weights and rhythms map a sense of organic growth onto a flat, structured page?
g1112.shape: How might the geometry of radiating forms connect natural study to the ornamental interests of its era?
g1112.color: How does the chromatic system of the plate serve classification and pleasure at the same time?
g1112.texture: How does the lithographic tonality negotiate between a specimen's physical surface and a stylized surface?
g1112.space: How does the compression of many forms into a shallow, patterned space differ from a naturalistic habitat view?
g1112.light: How does the modulation of light preserve a sense of translucent living tissue within a controlled design?
g1112.meaning: Haeckel's broader scientific ideas have been debated. How should a viewer weigh the beauty of this image against such debates?
g1112.culture: How did print culture around 1904 make such images widely circulated, and how might circulation shape authority?
g1112.technique: How does the lithographic technique, as seen in the fine transitions, affect your trust in the image as evidence?
g1112.personal: How does your own training or interests shape whether you see this plate as science, art or design first?
g1112.critical: What would a rigorous critique of the line between illustration and idealization look like, using this plate as evidence?

teacherNote.context: A lithography print from 1904 by Ernst Haeckel showing sea anemones, grouped under the Latin name Actiniae. The plate is part of the Art Forms in Nature series.
directions: Have students sketch one anemone by starting with a central circle and adding repeating tentacles, then compare how the radial pattern looks in different drawings.
Ask students to sort what they see on the plate into 'looks like science' and 'looks like design' and discuss where the two overlap.
Compare this plate with a modern photograph of a sea anemone and discuss what each kind of image can and cannot show.
